name: Umar Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time, Umar. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. What you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Can you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run an electric rope shovel at an oil sands mine. The oil sands are a thick layer of sand soaked in heavy oil, and the shovel is a giant digger, the bucket takes about a hundred tonnes a scoop, that fills the trucks that carry it to the plant. Twelve-hour shifts, four on, four off, and in winter it's dark when you start and dark when you finish. I like that it's a skill, you're reading the face, keeping the floor flat, loading a truck in three passes if you're good, four if you're average, and I'm usually four. What wears me out is the cold in the mornings, and the boredom when the trucks are slow and you're just waiting.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live in a duplex I bought two years ago, I live in one half and rent out the other. I've got savings on top of that, more than a year. My older brother Yusuf and I run a small side business in winter, clearing snow from car parks and driveways with two skid steers, those are small loaders. I go to the mosque on Fridays when I'm not on shift, and my parents live ten minutes away, I eat with them most days off. I use AI every day, for the business invoices, for routing the snow jobs, for reading machine manuals, everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was oversold, but the tools are still good for small things. At work I'd tell the guys I still use it for the side business every day. I'd probably post something like, it's a tool, not a miracle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it doesn't change much. The mine's been trialling driverless haul trucks for years, AI or not, so that keeps going. My shovel job is fine for now, and the side business keeps growing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working the shovel and keep using AI to run the snow business, maybe add a third skid steer this winter. I'd keep putting money into the duplex and look for another property in a year or two. Nothing really changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Business as usual.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How did the snow business start?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yusuf had a skid steer for his landscaping work in summer, and one winter a neighbour asked if he'd clear the car park at the medical centre. I set up the booking and invoices with AI on my phone that night. Now we've got forty customers, and I do the whole admin side in about twenty minutes a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do your parents think of all of it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad drove a taxi for thirty years, he worked six days a week so we could have more than he did. He's proud, but he says don't forget the mosque and don't forget your mother. He doesn't trust the AI, he thinks it'll make me lazy.

S0.say: He'd say AI was oversold but still good for small things, tell crewmates he uses it daily for his side business and post that it's a tool, not a miracle.
S0.think: He thinks it doesn't change much for him, since driverless trucks are being trialled anyway and his shovel job is fine for now. The side business keeps growing.
S0.do: Keeps working the shovel and running the snow business with AI, possibly adding a third skid steer this winter. Keeps paying into the duplex and looks for another property within a year or two.
S0.quote: Now we've got forty customers, and I do the whole admin side in about twenty minutes a week.
S0.fieldNote: Umar already thinks like a small business owner; he and his brother run forty snow-clearing customers, with AI doing the admin. His father's hard work as a taxi driver anchors his values of family and faith. Even in a quiet AI world, he keeps building assets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance for people who are willing to work and learn. At work I'd be encouraging people to pick up the tools, not wait for the government to sort it out. Online I'd share stories of people who made it work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think the shovel's going to go semi-automatic within a few years, with one person watching three from a control room. Maybe that's me, maybe not, I'm only average with the bucket. Either way, it's a good moment to grow the business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd buy a third skid steer and look at the ones that can be driven remotely or run on a set path, so one of us can run two at once. I'd put my hand up for the shovel remote training at the mine because it's paid and it looks good on my record. I'd also look at a second duplex, because rent keeps coming in whatever happens to my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd bring automation into your own business. Does it bother you that it might cost someone else a job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, honestly. We're two brothers, we'd just be doing more with the same two people. If I don't put a robot on my car parks, the big company from the city will put theirs, and then neither of us has the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the mine would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's a guy on my crew, Pete, he's been on the shovel twenty-two years. He says he'll retire before he touches a screen. I'd tell him to learn it anyway, but he's got his house paid off, so he might be fine.

S1.say: He'd call it a chance for people willing to work and learn, encourage coworkers to pick up the tools rather than wait for the government, and share success stories online.
S1.think: He thinks the shovel will go semi-automatic within a few years, with one operator watching three; as an average operator he might not be the one kept. Either way he sees a good moment to grow the business.
S1.do: Buys a third skid steer in the first year, looking at models that run remotely or on a set path, and volunteers for paid shovel remote training. Looks into buying a second duplex for rental income.
S1.quote: If I don't put a robot on my car parks, the big company from the city will put theirs, and then neither of us has the work.
S1.fieldNote: Umar is willing to automate his own small business, arguing that if he doesn't, a bigger city company will. His free-market view comes through as 'don't wait for government'. He's honest about being only average on the shovel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shock, but people need to stand up and look after their own families, not wait for handouts. At the mosque I'd say we have to look after each other, the old way. Online I'd post less, honestly, I'd be busy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it'd worry me. If AI can do anything, my shovel job goes, but so does the snow business, because the city companies will have robot snow ploughs before we can afford them. I've got the duplex and the savings, so I'd survive, but my whole plan was to grow the business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop any new buying straight away, no third skid steer, no second duplex, and keep the cash. If I'd already taken a loan for a machine, I'd try to pay it off fast or sell the machine. I'd sit down with Yusuf and my dad and work out together what the family does, maybe pool our money into one property everyone can rely on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not scared for my food, scared for my plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years' warning, what would you do before it arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Squeeze the last winters out of the snow business and save every cent. Two years is two winters. You can't build a business in two winters, you can only shut one down properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said pooling money with family. Is that something your family has done before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, when my parents bought their house, my uncles all put in. That's how we've always done it. If the jobs go, family's still there.

S2.say: He'd call it a shock but say people should look after their own families rather than wait for handouts, and at the mosque he'd say everyone must look after each other the old way. He'd post less online because he'd be busy.
S2.think: It would worry him, since both the shovel job and the snow business would go, with city companies getting robot ploughs first. The duplex and savings mean he'd survive, but his whole plan to grow the business would be finished.
S2.do: Stops new purchases, cancelling the third skid steer and second duplex, and pays off or sells any machine bought on a loan. Plans with Yusuf and his father to pool family money into one property they can all rely on, and works the last two winters hard to save.
S2.feel: Anxious, not for food but for his plans.
S2.quote: Two years is two winters. You can't build a business in two winters, you can only shut one down properly.
S2.fieldNote: For Umar, fast AGI wipes out the timeline his business strategy depended on. He turns immediately to family, describing a tradition of uncles pooling money for a house. His adaptability shows as fast retreat and consolidation rather than panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for people who are ready to work at it. At work I'd tell people to start something on the side now. At the mosque I'd say the same, use the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years feels okay for me. I'd have time to grow the snow business, buy the machines that run themselves, and own something that earns while I'm not there. It's tight, but doable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd buy two remote-capable skid steers and add a summer side to the business, maybe lawn and car park maintenance. By year two or three I'd cut back to fewer shifts at the mine to focus on the business. I'd keep the duplex and maybe buy the second one, because property still matters if robots are doing the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more busy than worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years change compared with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five winters instead of two. In five years I can own the robots. In two years I'm just racing them. That's the difference.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't owning robots exactly what you said the big city companies would do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, and that's why I'd want to do it first. I'd be small, local, people know me and my brother. They'd rather pay us than a company they've never met, at least for a while.

S3.say: He'd say five years is enough for people ready to work at it and tell people at work and the mosque to start something on the side now.
S3.think: He thinks five years feels okay for him: time to grow the snow business, buy self-running machines and own something that earns while he's away. It's tight but doable.
S3.do: Buys two remote-capable skid steers in the first year and adds summer lawn and car park maintenance. Cuts back mine shifts by year two or three to focus on the business and may buy the second duplex.
S3.feel: Uneasy, but more busy than worried.
S3.quote: In five years I can own the robots. In two years I'm just racing them.
S3.fieldNote: Five years flips his stance from defence to attack: he wants to own robots before the big companies arrive locally. He relies on being known in his community as a competitive edge. He sees property as a safe bet even in a robot-run world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a big opportunity, and people shouldn't waste it. At work I'd be the one telling younger guys to start a business. Online I'd post about what we're building.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think ten years is perfect for me. I'd be thirty-seven, with a solid business and a couple of properties, and machines doing a lot of the work. I'd still worry for people who don't plan, but I'd be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working the shovel for a few years while growing the business. Add remote-capable machines over the first three or four years and expand into summer work. Around year five, leave the mine and run the business full-time with Yusuf, maybe hire a cousin or two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and kind of excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you leave the mine earlier or later?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the business was bringing in more than the shovel, I'd go. If the business slowed down, I'd stay longer, the mine pays well. My dad drove someone else's taxi for thirty years. I want my kids to see me own the machines, not drive them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And if things went badly for people in the town, who would you hold responsible?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly people who had ten years and did nothing. I don't like blaming government for everything. But the big companies should have to play fair, so the small guys get a chance.

S4.say: He'd call ten years a big opportunity not to be wasted, urge younger crewmates to start businesses and post online about what he's building.
S4.think: He thinks ten years is perfect for him, landing at thirty-seven with a solid business, a couple of properties and machines doing much of the work. He'd worry for people who don't plan but be fine himself.
S4.do: Keeps working the shovel for a few years while adding remote-capable machines and summer work to the business. Around year five, leaves the mine to run the business full-time with Yusuf and possibly hires cousins.
S4.quote: My dad drove someone else's taxi for thirty years. I want my kids to see me own the machines, not drive them.
S4.fieldNote: His ten-year plan is driven by a family story: his father drove someone else's taxi, and Umar wants to own the machines. He places most responsibility on individuals who waste time but wants fair rules against big companies. His free-market and family values work together here.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Not because I'd go hungry, but because everything I've been building would be cut off before it got going. What would help is rules that stop the big companies from crushing the small local ones, and cheap loans for small businesses to buy the new machines. Don't give me a payment. Give me a fair chance to own a piece of the new thing.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about family. Everyone talks about jobs, but for us the plan was always family first. Whatever happens with robots, Yusuf and I will figure it out together.

headlineQuote: Don't give me a payment. Give me a fair chance to own a piece of the new thing.
portrait: Umar is a 27-year-old electric rope shovel operator at an oil sands mine who owns a duplex, rents out half of it and has more than a year's savings. He uses AI every day to run a winter snow-clearing business with his brother Yusuf, and his father's thirty years driving someone else's taxi drive his wish to own things. Across the scenarios he wants to automate his own business before big city companies do, and he leans on family and his mosque rather than government. Only AGI in two years makes him anxious, because there'd be no time to build; with ten years he plans to leave the mine and run the business full-time.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because everything he's been building would be cut off before it got going.
whatWouldHelp: Rules that stop big companies crushing small local firms, and cheap loans so small businesses can buy the new machines.
